title: Time Based Key-Value Store
description: Brute force to optimized: scanning every stored value for a key on every get versus binary searching its already-sorted timestamp history.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Design a time-based key-value store, supporting set(key, value, timestamp), which stores the value for key at the given time, and get(key, timestamp), which returns the value associated with key at the largest recorded timestamp that is less than or equal to the given timestamp (or an empty string if none exists).

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","A sequence of set and get calls"],["Output","The result of every get call"],["Goal","Answer get quickly, even with many stored values per key"],["Constraints","Timestamps passed to set are strictly increasing for each key; up to 200000 total calls"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["Timestamps for a given key are always set in strictly increasing order","The stored list of timestamps for each key is already sorted, no extra sorting needed"],["A get query needs \"the latest entry at or before a given time\"","Binary search for the rightmost timestamp not exceeding the query"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

Maintain, for every key, a history of (timestamp, value) pairs. A get(key, timestamp) query should return the value from the latest set call for that key whose timestamp does not exceed the query timestamp.

blocks.title: Analogy: Looking Up a Value From a Version History
blocks.text: Picture a document's edit history, where each edit is timestamped and only ever added at the end (since edits happen in real time). Looking up "what did this document say at this earlier point in time" means finding the latest edit that had already happened by then.

blocks.caption: Timestamps arrive already sorted; binary search finds the answer directly

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: set("foo","bar",1), get("foo",1), get("foo",3)
get("foo",1) returns "bar" (set exactly at that timestamp); get("foo",3) also returns "bar", since no later value exists yet and 1 is still the latest timestamp not exceeding 3.
Example continued: set("foo","bar2",4), get("foo",4), get("foo",5)
Both return "bar2", the latest value at or before their respective query timestamps.
5. How Should We Think?
Before scanning every stored value for a key, notice that since set calls for a key always use strictly increasing timestamps, the stored history for that key is already sorted by construction.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Storing a list of (timestamp, value) pairs per key, appended in the order set is called, results in a list already sorted by timestamp, since the problem guarantees strictly increasing timestamps per key.

Observation 2: A get query needs the rightmost timestamp in that sorted list that does not exceed the query, exactly the kind of boundary a binary search finds directly.

Observation 3: Binary searching for "the first timestamp greater than the query" and stepping back one position gives exactly that rightmost valid entry.

Observation 4: If the query timestamp is smaller than every stored timestamp for that key, no valid entry exists, and an empty string is returned.
This leads to storing each key's history as an append-only, already-sorted list, and using binary search on get to find the latest qualifying value.
6. Brute Force Solution
Store every (timestamp, value) pair for a key in a list. On get, scan the entire list, tracking the best qualifying value found.
Step by step algorithm

items: set(key, value, timestamp): append (timestamp, value) to that key's list.
get(key, timestamp): scan every (t, v) pair for that key, tracking the one with the largest t that is still at most the query timestamp.
Return the best value found, or an empty string if none qualify.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: scan every stored value for the key on every get

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every (timestamp, value) pair for a key is examined on every get call, regardless of how many there are.
The already-sorted nature of the stored list (guaranteed by strictly increasing set timestamps) is never actually used to skip any comparisons.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(m) per get, where m is the number of values stored for that key.
Space: O(n), storing every set call ever made.
Limitation: the stored list for a key is already sorted by timestamp, since set calls arrive in strictly increasing order, but a linear scan does not exploit that at all.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why a linear scan is unnecessary: the list of timestamps for a given key is already sorted, by the problem's own guarantee, so the "latest timestamp at or before the query" boundary can be found directly.

What binary search finds: the first stored timestamp strictly greater than the query; the entry just before it is exactly the answer.

The core idea: on get, binary search the key's sorted timestamp list for that boundary, instead of scanning every entry.

Store each key's history as a list of (timestamp, value) pairs, appended in set-call order (already sorted). On get, binary search for the first timestamp strictly greater than the query, and return the value just before that position, or an empty string if the query is smaller than every stored timestamp.
9. Optimized Solution
Dry run for key "foo" with history [(1,"bar"), (4,"bar2")], get(timestamp=3)

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result"],"rows":[["Binary search for first timestamp > 3","found at index 1 (timestamp 4)"],["Step back one position","index 0, value \"bar\""]]}

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: binary search the sorted timestamp list directly

blocks.text: Why This Works

Since set calls for a key always use strictly increasing timestamps, the stored list is already sorted with no extra work. Binary searching for the first timestamp strictly greater than the query directly locates the boundary; the entry just before it is guaranteed to be the latest one at or before the query, exactly the answer required.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(log m) per get, where m is the number of values stored for that key; O(1) per set.
Space: O(n), storing every set call ever made.
10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Solution","get time","set time","Interview Recommendation"],"rows":[["Brute force (linear scan per get)","O(m)","O(1)","Correct, but slows as more values accumulate per key."],["Optimized (binary search per get)","O(log m)","O(1)","The expected answer, a genuine complexity class improvement."]]}

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

The key insight is recognizing that the problem's own guarantee, strictly increasing timestamps per key, means no sorting is ever needed; a plain append-only list is already sorted, and get becomes a direct binary search for the "latest at or before" boundary.
Common Mistakes

items: Re-sorting the stored list on every get, unnecessary since it is already sorted by construction.
Searching for an exact timestamp match instead of the latest one at or before the query.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["get called before any set for that key","Returns an empty string."],["get with a timestamp smaller than every stored one for that key","Returns an empty string."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips

Pointing out explicitly that the problem's constraint (strictly increasing timestamps per set call) removes any need to sort is a small but important detail worth stating before writing the binary search.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "can you avoid scanning every stored value", think: the list is already sorted by timestamp, binary search for the boundary directly.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you support a "delete" operation on this store?
How would this change if timestamps were not guaranteed to be strictly increasing per key?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Any "append-only, naturally sorted history, binary search for a boundary" design problem.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs get in O(m) time; the optimized binary search runs get in O(log m) time. Both run set in O(1) time and use O(n) total space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: an append-only, naturally sorted history per key, searched with binary search.
Core Idea: since timestamps arrive in strictly increasing order, the stored list is already sorted; get is a binary search for the latest entry at or before the query.
Time: O(m) per get for the brute force, O(log m) for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: the problem's own guarantee about increasing timestamps means the data is already sorted, no extra work is needed to keep it that way.
Interview Difficulty: straightforward once the "already sorted, just binary search" insight is recognized.
One line memory trick: already sorted by construction; binary search for the latest at or before.
